description: Primacy and recency effects, the serial position curve, and Murdock's word-list study.
content_html:
Serial Position and Recall

If someone reads you a list of twenty words and asks you to recall them in any order, the position of each word in the list affects how likely you are to remember it. This is called the serial position effect. Psychologists have found two consistent patterns in this effect: you tend to remember words at the beginning of the list (the primacy effect) and words at the end of the list (the recency effect) better than words in the middle.

Key Fact

The primacy effect refers to better recall of items at the start of a list; the recency effect refers to better recall of items at the end. The primacy effect is explained by transfer to long-term memory via rehearsal; the recency effect is explained by items still being active in short-term memory.

The Primacy Effect

The primacy effect occurs because the first few items on a list receive the most rehearsal. When you hear the first word, there is nothing else competing for your attention in short-term memory, so you repeat it several times. By the time the list is over, those early words have been rehearsed enough to be transferred into long-term memory, where they can be retrieved later. Words in the middle of the list receive less rehearsal because STM is quickly filled by new incoming items.

The Recency Effect

The recency effect occurs because the last few words on the list are the most recently heard and are still being held in short-term memory at the time of recall. They have not had time to fade. However, the recency effect is fragile: if there is a delay before recall, or if participants are asked to do a distracting task between hearing the list and recalling it, the recency effect disappears because STM trace has faded. The primacy effect remains because those early words are safely in LTM.

When psychologists plot the probability of recall against the position of each word in a list, the result is a U-shaped graph called the serial position curve. Recall is high for the first few words (primacy), drops in the middle, and rises again for the last few words (recency). This characteristic shape appears consistently across many free recall studies.

Murdock’s Serial Position Curve Study

The most important study in this area is Murdock’s (1962) investigation of the serial position effect. It is a named study you need to know in detail: aim, method, results, and conclusion.

Key Fact

Murdock (1962): Aim — to investigate the serial position effect in free recall. Method — participants heard lists of words (typically 20 words, presented at a rate of one word per second) and were asked to recall them in any order immediately afterwards. Results — words at the start (primacy) and end (recency) were recalled better than words in the middle; a U-shaped serial position curve was produced. Conclusion — the pattern supports the idea of separate STM and LTM stores.

A strength of Murdock’s study is that it used a controlled laboratory method, which allows replication and high internal validity — extraneous variables such as word length and presentation rate were carefully controlled. The study produced consistent, replicable results that have been repeated many times, supporting its reliability.

A weakness is that the task was artificial: memorising lists of unrelated words has little resemblance to everyday memory tasks. This reduces ecological validity — results may not reflect how memory works in real life. The study also used participants in a restricted setting, which may limit how far findings generalise to all people and all types of memory task.

Link to the Multi-Store Model

The serial position curve provides evidence for the multi-store model of memory. The primacy effect demonstrates that rehearsal can transfer information into long-term memory — early items are recalled from LTM. The recency effect demonstrates the existence of a separate, limited short-term store — end items are recalled directly from STM. When a delay is introduced before recall, the recency effect disappears but the primacy effect remains, which is exactly what the multi-store model would predict: STM traces fade quickly while LTM traces persist.

Why Middle Items Are Recalled Poorly

It is worth understanding precisely why items in the middle of a list are the hardest to recall. When you hear the first few words, your STM is relatively empty and you can rehearse them repeatedly. But as more words arrive, your STM fills to its limited capacity of around seven items. New words displace older ones before those older words have had enough rehearsal to reach LTM. At the same time, the middle items are not the most recent, so they are no longer active in STM at the point of recall. The result is that they fall through the gap between the two stores and are lost.

This competition between new and old items in a limited-capacity store is sometimes called displacement. Each new item in a full STM pushes out the item that has been there longest without sufficient rehearsal to move it to LTM. Middle items receive neither the rehearsal advantage of early items nor the recency advantage of final items, which is why the serial position curve dips in the middle.

The displacement account is consistent with the multi-store model’s claim that STM has a fixed capacity of around seven items (plus or minus two). If STM had unlimited capacity, every item would have as much opportunity for rehearsal as the first item, and there would be no primacy advantage — the serial position curve would be flat, not U-shaped.
exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark ‘describe a study’ question on Murdock, make sure you cover all four elements: aim, method, results and conclusion. A common mistake is giving only findings and skipping the aim or conclusion. For evaluation questions, do not just say ‘it lacked ecological validity’ — say WHY: because memorising lists of unrelated words is unlike real-world memory. Examiners want elaborated points, not bare labels.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The serial position effect shows that recall depends on where an item appears in a list: the primacy effect (start = LTM via rehearsal) and recency effect (end = still in STM) produce a characteristic U-shaped serial position curve.
  • Murdock (1962) demonstrated this using free recall of word lists under controlled laboratory conditions, finding better recall for items at the start and end than in the middle.
  • The serial position curve supports the multi-store model: the recency effect disappears after a delay (STM trace fades) while the primacy effect persists (LTM trace remains), confirming two separate stores.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly explains the recency effect?
A) Items at the start of a list are recalled because they were rehearsed into LTM
B) Items in the middle of a list are recalled because they are distinctive
C) Items at the end of a list are recalled because they are still active in STM
D) Items at the start of a list are recalled because they are still active in STM
practice_questions.marks: C) Items at the end of a list are recalled because they are still active in STM [1 mark]

Mastering: Precise definition stating that the primacy effect is the tendency to recall items at the beginning of a list better than those in the middle, because early items receive more rehearsal and are transferred to long-term memory.
Secure: Clear definition capturing ‘beginning of a list’ and ‘better recall’ with a link to rehearsal or LTM.
Developing: Identifies better recall for items at the start but does not explain why.
Emerging: Vague or confused with recency effect.

practice_questions.text: Describe what a serial position curve looks like and what it shows.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes the U-shaped curve with recall probability on the vertical axis and serial position on the horizontal; names both the primacy effect (high recall at start) and recency effect (high recall at end) with lower recall in the middle; explains what the shape shows about memory.
Secure: Describes the U-shape and names both effects.
Developing: Describes the shape or names one effect; the other is missing.
Emerging: Vague description without naming the effects or shape.

practice_questions.text: Describe Murdock's serial position curve study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Covers aim (to investigate serial position effect in free recall), method (participants heard word lists at a set rate, recalled in any order immediately after), results (U-shaped curve, primacy and recency effects, middle items recalled least), and conclusion (supports separate STM and LTM stores); precise psychological language used throughout.
Secure: All four elements present; one may lack full development.
Developing: Three elements present; one missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: Only finding or only aim mentioned; structure of study not evident.

practice_questions.text: Explain what would happen to the recency effect if participants were asked to count backwards for 30 seconds before recalling the word list. Use your knowledge of the multi-store model in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that the recency effect would disappear; explains that the distracting task prevents rehearsal and causes STM traces to fade; links to the multi-store model (STM has short duration without rehearsal); the primacy effect would remain because those items are already in LTM.
Secure: Correctly predicts disappearance of recency effect with clear reference to STM duration; primacy effect mentioned.
Developing: Predicts the recency effect changes but explanation of why is limited or does not clearly reference the multi-store model.
Emerging: Recognises a change but cannot explain it in terms of the model.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Murdock's serial position curve study.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Aim to investigate the serial position effect; participants heard word lists and recalled freely; results showed a U-shaped curve with better recall for early (primacy) and late (recency) items than middle items; conclusion supports separate STM and LTM stores.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — controlled laboratory study allows replication; extraneous variables controlled. Weakness — low ecological validity because memorising unrelated word lists is unlike everyday memory. Strength — results replicated consistently across many studies, supporting reliability. Weakness — limited to one type of memory task; may not reflect memory for meaningful material.
Mastering: Accurate full study description plus two or more developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Study described and two evaluation points made with some elaboration.
Developing: Study described with at least one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief or inaccurate description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

knowledge_checks.q: What shape does the serial position curve take?
options: A bell-shaped curve with highest recall in the middle
A U-shaped curve with highest recall at the start and end

knowledge_checks.q: Why does the primacy effect occur, according to the multi-store model?
options: Early items are the most surprising and therefore distinctive
Early items are still active in short-term memory at recall
Early items receive the most rehearsal and are transferred to long-term memory
Early items are encoded visually rather than acoustically

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ effect refers to the better recall of items at the end of a list because they are still active in short-term memory.
Murdock's (1962) study used a free _____ task, where participants heard word lists and recalled them in any order.
Match each serial position effect to its explanation:
right: Items still active in short-term memory at time of recall
STM is full, reducing rehearsal opportunities for mid-list items
Items transferred to long-term memory through repeated rehearsal

flashcard_questions.q: What is the serial position effect?
flashcard_questions.a: The finding that recall depends on where an item appears in a list.
Better recall of items at the start of a list, due to rehearsal transferring them to LTM.
Better recall of items at the end of a list, because they are still active in STM.

flashcard_questions.q: What shape does the serial position curve produce?
flashcard_questions.a: A U-shaped curve: high recall at start and end, lower in the middle.

flashcard_questions.q: Who conducted the classic serial position curve study and when?

flashcard_questions.a: To investigate the serial position effect in free recall of word lists.
A U-shaped curve: words at the start and end were recalled better than words in the middle.
The pattern of results supports the existence of separate STM and LTM stores.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the recency effect if there is a delay before recall?
flashcard_questions.a: It disappears, because the STM trace fades without rehearsal.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the primacy effect if there is a delay before recall?
flashcard_questions.a: It remains, because those items have been transferred to long-term memory.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one weakness of Murdock's study.
flashcard_questions.a: Low ecological validity: memorising unrelated word lists is unlike real-world memory tasks.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is recall poorest for items in the middle of a list, according to the multi-store model?
flashcard_questions.a: STM fills to capacity, so middle items are displaced before enough rehearsal to reach LTM, and are no longer recent enough to stay active.

glossary_terms.definition: The finding that a person's ability to recall an item from a list depends on where it appears in that list.
The tendency to recall items at the beginning of a list better than those in the middle, linked to transfer to long-term memory.
The tendency to recall items at the end of a list better than those in the middle, linked to items still being in short-term memory.
A U-shaped graph showing that items at the beginning and end of a list are recalled better than items in the middle.

hero_image_caption: Laboratory word-list tasks reveal how position in a sequence affects memory recall.
